newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN chief pledges transparency at human rights body.
newsitem.headline: UN chief pledges transparency at human rights body.

text.p: United Nations chief Kofi Annan promised on Wednesday to make the world body's cash-strapped human rights office more open and effective.

In a speech to the 53-member U.N. Human Rights Commission meeting in Geneva, the new secretary-general pledged to reform the rights office, which is often criticised by activists for its low-profile in dealing with governments accused of abuses.
But Annan did not elaborate how he would reform the body, and human rights activists criticised his speech as vague and non-committal.
"This effort will encompass increased transparency and the installing of a culture of sharing," Annan said.

"Gross violations of human rights invariably go hand-in-hand with situations that may threaten peace and security and are likely to degenerate into confrontation. U.N. work in the field of human rights... should be seen as... preventive diplomacy."
Annan did not say anything about plans to name a new human rights chief to replace Jose Ayala Lasso, a cautious career diplomat who quit in March to become Ecuador's foreign minister.

"We'd have liked to see some concrete steps announced," said Reed Brody of the Human Rights Internet group, a respected activist who was formerly head of human rights for the U.N. peacekeeping operation in El Salvador.
Brody said the office needed strong representation in New York to keep human rights concerns on the agenda of top U.N. officials and the U.N. Security Council.
Annan has named Ralph Zacklin, a U.N. legal officer, as caretaker for the job but human rights groups say the post is too important to be left vacant long.
The Irish government has nominated President Mary Robinson for the job when she leaves office at the end of 1997. Diplomats say it is doubtful the post could remain vacant until then.
The other declared candidate is Sonia Picado, Costa Rica's ambassador to Washington and the choice of Latin American and Caribbean states that want the post to stay in their region.
U.S. officials said Washington supported both women's candidacies.
The resolution creating the high-profile job in 1993 was vague on its duties because the West wanted an outspoken rights commissioner while some Third World countries wanted probes restricted.
The post has to be approved by the U.N. General Assembly, where developing nations hold a majority.
